solution: A giant leaves mountain i only once its damaged height falls strictly below a_{i+1}, which costs a_i - a_{i+1} + 1 boulders, and the final mountain costs a_n more. The sum telescopes, so defeating a giant takes exactly a_1 + n - 1 boulders no matter what the interior heights are. The giants alternate with the first one throwing first, so giant 1 wins iff b_1 + m - 1 <= a_1 + n - 1, i.e. only the tallest mountain and the mountain count matter. O(n + m) per test, which is just the input read; confirmed against a literal turn-by-turn simulation on the six samples and on 3000 random small cases.
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force

skeptic_rulings.label: game-theory
skeptic_rulings.why: Every one of the 35 existing carriers has a player making a choice - even the greedy ones. Here throws, jumps and resignation are all forced, so there is no strategy to analyse; the content is a telescoping count (a_1 + n - 1 boulders) and the winner is a two-line comparison. CF tags it math only. Domain recall survives via the tags field, which already carries game-theory.

notes: Neither player ever chooses anything: throws, jumps and resignation are all forced, so this is a closed-form math problem and not Sprague-Grundy analysis (the judge tags it 'math' only, not 'games'). The vocabulary has no plain 'math'/'observation' label; 'counting' stands for the telescoping boulder count, and 'game-theory' is kept only as the domain label for a two-player alternating-turn winner question, at low confidence. Deliberately no 'simulation': heights reach 1e9, so nothing can be stepped through move by move.
